No, that's not right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own. Each call starts blank, and the model sees only the text it's handed in that call. This ties to what you already worked out: it knows what it learned in training plus what's in its input. Chatbots seem to remember because the app re-sends the earlier messages with every new one.

Think of a rental car with no trip log. Every time you get in, it starts with no record of the last driver. If you want it to "remember" the seat position, something outside the car has to store the setting and apply it each time you sit down.

For your assistant, that outside part is your Python code:

- At the end of a session, your program saves what matters, such as a student's training status, to a file or database.
- At the start of the next session, your program looks it up and puts it into the text it sends to the model.
- If your program doesn't do both, the model has no idea last week happened.

The "what does it save between sessions" goal in your mission is a design decision for you, not something the model handles. It also affects cost, because everything you re-send is input you pay for. So you'll want to save short facts, not whole transcripts.

Quick check: a student says "I'm certified on the 3D printers" on Monday, and you save nothing. On Friday they ask "can I book one?" What does the model have to go on?

When you're ready, I can build a lesson on context and memory. It's next in your mission, and I'd include a small hands-on demo.
